Cross-Channel Journey Stitching — Internal Case Review

Case Review Dashboard

Every card member's activity across app, web, phone, and branch, stitched into one story. Use this to find where an experience broke down, see a customer's full history before you call them back, and check why the system believes two interactions are the same person.

How to read this
Risk score
0–100, combining how many times a customer switched channels, how long the issue has been open, repeat phone contact, and whether it's resolved. Above 65 enters the review queue; above 85 triggers an alert.
Case ID vs. raw ID
"Case #12" is a friendly label for this dashboard. The CONFIRMED-EVT-… code beneath it is the system's actual identifier — use it if you need to cross-reference elsewhere.
Identity Merge Audit
Shows why the system believes two interactions belong to the same person. "Deterministic" means certain (same account login, phone number on file, etc). "Probabilistic" means likely, not certain. "Tiebreaker" (e.g. shared IP address) is recorded for reference only — it never merges two people on its own, since a shared home network isn't proof of identity.
6ms

is how long it took Sarah's failed app dispute to become queryable in the real-time store — 90 seconds before she even finished dialing.

Scene 1 — the agent already knows

Sarah is traveling. She opens the Amex app to dispute a $200 charge she doesn't recognize — her connection drops mid-submission. Ninety seconds later, she calls support.

“Hi Sarah — I see you were just trying to dispute a $200 charge on the app a few seconds ago. I have the details right here. Are you safe?”

Why the agent already knew

This customer is still unresolved. The score isn't dramatic here — correctly. It rewards accumulated risk (repeat contacts, elapsed unresolved time), and a case that's one channel-switch old hasn't built any up yet. What actually changed this call wasn't an alert — it was the agent having her timeline already open.

Scene 2 — the pattern behind the Sarahs who aren't saved

Sarah's own two-event case is too short to register as a risk pattern on its own — and it shouldn't, she was helped immediately. But she isn't the only card member whose app dispute fails and who then calls. Some of those calls don't get resolved on the first try. That's the same pattern, surfacing automatically, in the aggregate:
